plan: SAT R&W batch 70: 9 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000626..000634, weighted toward hard (Tycho Brahe WIC, Kirtland's warbler inference, street-tree temperature quantitative comparison of differences, Walden quotation evidence, Chien-Shiung Wu purpose, Sequoyah agreement, Fazlur Khan colon, Zitkala-Sa transition, Fanny Hesse agar synthesis). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Plus S069-06 resubmitted as revision 2 (hint reworded) on its previously unbanked passage. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A new star
passages.text: Before 1572, most European astronomers held that the heavens beyond the Moon were ______: weather and seasons might change on Earth, but the stars were thought to remain exactly as they had always been. That November, the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe observed a brilliant new star in the constellation Cassiopeia and showed, through careful measurements, that it lay far beyond the Moon.

passages.title: Young forests
passages.text: Kirtland's warblers nest almost exclusively in young stands of jack pine, typically between about 5 and 20 years old, growing on sandy soils in northern Michigan. In the past, wildfires regularly cleared old jack pine forests, and new stands sprang up in their place. During the twentieth century, as people increasingly put out wildfires, young stands became scarce, and in 1974 surveyors counted only about 167 singing males. Since then, managers have harvested and replanted thousands of acres of jack pine each year. Based on the text, this approach is most likely intended to ______

passages.title: Shade on the street
passages.text:
On a summer afternoon, a student measured the average surface temperature of sidewalks on three types of streets in her city.
No trees: 48°C
A few trees: 41°C
Continuous tree canopy: 33°C
The student claims that the drop in temperature between streets with a few trees and streets with a continuous canopy was larger than the drop between streets with no trees and streets with a few trees.

passages.title: A purposeful retreat
passages.text: From 1845 to 1847, Henry David Thoreau lived in a small cabin he had built near Walden Pond in Massachusetts, an experience he described in Walden (1854). Thoreau presents his stay as a purposeful experiment, undertaken to discover what life, reduced to its essentials, could teach him.

passages.title: Left and right
passages.text: In 1956, physicists Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang proposed that a long-accepted principle, that nature makes no distinction between left and right, might not hold for certain particle interactions. Later that year, the physicist Chien-Shiung Wu designed an experiment using cobalt-60 atoms cooled to near absolute zero and found that the atoms emitted electrons more often in one direction than the other, showing that the principle did fail. Lee and Yang received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics; Wu was not included.

passages.title: A writing system
passages.text: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith, completed a writing system for the Cherokee language in 1821. Each of the system's symbols ______ a syllable, which made it unusually quick to learn: within a few years, thousands of Cherokee people could read and write in their own language.

passages.title: Tall and light
passages.text: In the 1960s, the structural engineer Fazlur Khan developed the "tube" system, in which a building's closely spaced outer columns work together like a hollow tube to resist the wind. The system made very tall buildings far cheaper to construct, and Khan used versions of it in two of Chicago's best-known ______ the John Hancock Center and the Sears Tower (now the Willis Tower).

passages.title: A school far from home
passages.text: In 1900, the Yankton Dakota writer Zitkala-Ša published essays in the Atlantic Monthly about the boarding school she had attended as a child, where Native students were pressured to give up their languages and customs. ______ she recalled being forced to have her long hair cut, which in her community was associated with mourners or cowards.

passages.title: Notes on a kitchen discovery
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1880s, scientists growing bacteria often used gelatin as a solid surface.
- Gelatin melts at warm temperatures, and some bacteria break it down.
- Fanny Hesse, who assisted her husband, the physician Walther Hesse, in his laboratory, suggested using agar instead.
- She had used agar to make jellies in her kitchen.
- Agar stays solid at body temperature, and few bacteria can break it down.
- Agar is still widely used to grow bacteria in laboratories.

passages.title: A map of the world in clay
passages.text: Among the oldest known attempts to map the whole world ______ the Babylonian Map of the World, a small clay tablet from about the sixth century BCE that shows the city of Babylon surrounded by a circular ocean.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: the stars were thought to remain exactly as they had always been
candidates.explanation: The astronomers believed the stars never changed, so they held the heavens to be "immutable" (unchanging).

A.rationale: The text is about whether the heavens change, not whether they can be understood.

B.rationale: Whether the heavens could support life is not discussed.

D.rationale: The stars were visible; the belief concerned whether they changed.

hints: What did astronomers believe about change in the heavens?

strategy.explanation: Predict "unchanging" from the text after the colon.

candidates.remember: Use the explanation after a colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: replace a habitat that wildfires once created.
choices.B: eliminate wildfires entirely from the warbler's range.
choices.C: encourage the warblers to nest in older forests instead.
choices.D: increase the number of jack pines that reach old age.

candidates.explanation: Fires once produced the young stands the warblers need; with fires suppressed, harvesting and replanting produces those stands instead.

B.rationale: The text does not say the replanting is meant to stop fires.

C.rationale: The replanting creates young stands, not older forests.

D.rationale: Harvesting and replanting produces young trees, not old ones.

hints: What did fires used to do for the warblers?

strategy.explanation: Connect the managers' action to what was lost.

candidates.remember: An inference should link the evidence directly.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Sidewalks on streets with a continuous tree canopy were 15°C cooler, on average, than sidewalks on streets with no trees at all.
choices.B: Sidewalks on streets with no trees were the hottest of the three types measured, at an average of 48°C.
choices.C: Sidewalks on streets with a few trees were 7°C cooler than sidewalks on streets with no trees.
choices.D: Sidewalks were 8°C cooler under a continuous canopy than with a few trees, but only 7°C cooler with a few trees than with none.

candidates.evidence: was larger than the drop between streets with no trees
candidates.explanation: The claim compares two drops: 41 − 33 = 8 and 48 − 41 = 7. Only this choice gives both and shows that the first is larger.

A.rationale: This compares the extremes and does not compare the two drops.

B.rationale: This gives one value and does not compare the two drops.

C.rationale: This gives only one of the two drops the claim compares.

hints: How many differences does the claim compare?
candidates.remember: Support a comparison with both quantities being compared.

candidates.stem: Which quotation from Walden most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society."
choices.B: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach."
choices.C: "Our life is frittered away by detail. An honest man has hardly need to count more than his ten fingers, or in extreme cases he may add his ten toes, and lump the rest."
choices.D: "The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. What is called resignation is confirmed desperation."

candidates.evidence: a purposeful experiment, undertaken to discover what life, reduced to its essentials, could teach him
candidates.explanation: Only this quotation gives a purpose ("live deliberately"), a focus on essentials, and an aim to learn what life "had to teach."

A.rationale: This describes his furniture and visitors, not the purpose of his stay.

C.rationale: This criticizes complicated living but does not present the stay as an experiment meant to learn something.

D.rationale: This comments on other people's lives, not on the purpose of Thoreau's stay.

hints: Which parts of the claim must the quotation show?

strategy.explanation: Match each part of the claim to the quotation.

candidates.remember: The best quotation matches every part of the claim.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that Lee and Yang's proposal was mistaken and that Wu's careful experiment later disproved it
choices.B: To explain in detail how atoms of cobalt-60 can be cooled to temperatures near absolute zero for experiments
choices.C: To describe an experiment that confirmed a bold proposal and note that its designer did not share the prize
choices.D: To compare the careers of three physicists, each of whom later won a Nobel Prize for the research described

candidates.evidence: showing that the principle did fail
candidates.explanation: The text presents Lee and Yang's proposal, Wu's experiment confirming it, and the fact that the prize went to Lee and Yang but not Wu.

A.rationale: Wu's results supported the proposal; they did not disprove it.

B.rationale: The cooling is mentioned only briefly; the text does not explain how it is done.

D.rationale: The text says Wu was not included in the prize, and it does not compare careers.

hints: What does the text do from beginning to end?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The subject is "Each," which is singular, so the singular verb "stands for" is needed.

B.rationale: The subject is the singular "Each," not the plural "symbols."

C.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with the singular "Each."

D.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with the singular "Each."

strategy.explanation: Cross out the prepositional phrase "of the system's symbols."

candidates.subskill: Colon before a list or explanation
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the John Hancock Center and the Sears Tower
candidates.explanation: A colon after the complete clause correctly introduces the two buildings that "skyscrapers" refers to.

A.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but the two names are not one.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the names run directly into "skyscrapers."

hints: What follows the blank, and is it a clause?

strategy.explanation: Check what each side of the blank needs.

candidates.remember: A colon can introduce a list after a complete clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: forced to have her long hair cut
candidates.explanation: The second sentence gives a specific example of the pressure described in the first, so "Specifically" fits.

A.rationale: The haircut does not contrast with the pressure to give up customs; it is an instance of it.

C.rationale: The haircut is a specific case of the pressure, not a separate similar point.

D.rationale: The haircut does not replace anything described in the previous sentence.

hints: How does the second sentence relate to the first?
candidates.remember: Use "Specifically" to introduce a particular instance.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why agar was an improvement over gelatin. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Fanny Hesse, who assisted her husband in his laboratory, had used agar to make jellies in her kitchen before suggesting it to him and his colleagues.
choices.B: In the 1880s, scientists who wanted to grow bacteria on a solid surface in their laboratories often used gelatin for that purpose.
choices.C: Agar, which Fanny Hesse suggested in the 1880s, is still widely used today in laboratories around the world to grow bacteria.
choices.D: Unlike gelatin, which melts when warm and is broken down by some bacteria, agar stays solid at body temperature and resists most bacteria.

candidates.evidence: Agar stays solid at body temperature
candidates.explanation: Only this choice compares the two materials and gives the properties that make agar better.

A.rationale: This explains where the idea came from, not why agar is better.

B.rationale: This describes gelatin's use but not agar's advantages.

C.rationale: This shows agar's lasting use but does not compare it with gelatin.

hints: Which choice compares agar with gelatin?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must accomplish the stated goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the Babylonian Map of the World, a small clay tablet
candidates.explanation: In this inverted sentence the subject is "the Babylonian Map of the World," which is singular, so the singular "is" is needed.

A.rationale: The subject is the singular "Map," which follows the verb, not the plural "attempts."

B.rationale: The plural verb does not agree with the singular subject "Map."

D.rationale: A sentence needs a finite verb; "being" leaves it without one.

hints: Which noun does the verb have to agree with?

strategy.explanation: Reorder the sentence: "The Babylonian Map ... is among ..."

candidates.remember: In an inverted sentence, find the subject after the verb.

revision_history.reason: review tool: hint contained the key word "is" (possible giveaway)
